problem.statement: Originating a loan takes two pairs of hands, and the paper process had no safe way to hand over: consents got signed unread, documents arrived days late, and mistakes cost the customer a second visit.
bullets: Three roles run the process all day: sales centre executives, call centre executives and store managers.
The customer never touches the process except at the steps only they can complete, and every one of those is legally binding.
On paper those steps meant wet signatures, photocopied ID and consent forms collected out of sequence.
Six products each ran their own version of this, so nothing built for one could be reused by another.

background.title: Six products, three roles, and one moment that matters most.
bullets: FinVista is a consumer lending app for a large Indian NBFC, serving borrowers across more than 500 cities.
It is an **assisted** product. Executives drive it; the customer is sitting beside them, not holding the phone.
I led UX across six lending products and used the highest-volume one, the **two-wheeler loan**, as the proving ground.
The brief was an app. The real job was the handoff.

baseline: fields an executive keys in per application
moments only the customer can complete
of consents and signatures captured on paper
the weakest mobile coverage it still had to work on
audit: Nothing on paper marked where the executive's work stopped and the customer's began. Consent forms were signed in a stack, out of order, and afterwards nobody could tell which the customer had actually read.
Severity 4 · Match with the real world
Consent written for auditors, handed to a stranger
Bureau check and key facts language was drafted for compliance review, then put in front of someone with sixty seconds and a pen. Legally collected, not in any real sense understood.
Every competitor assumed one pair of hands

I pulled apart five of the leading Indian lending apps. Each handles a single product well and every one assumes the person holding the phone is the person applying. None had a model for passing the device across a desk mid-flow.
A mistyped field cost the customer a second trip
A wrong PAN or pin code surfaced days later at verification. The executive had made the error, and the customer had to come back to the store to fix it.

insight.title: The app belongs to the executive. Its most important minutes belong to a stranger.
bullets: An executive sees these screens hundreds of times. A customer sees them **about eight times, for under a minute each**, and only ever at the point of committing to something.
Live photo, KYC consent, bureau check consent, OTP, uploads, e-signature, home visit consent. Every one is legally binding and none of them can be delegated.
So I stopped designing one interface and started designing two modes of the same journey: **work mode** and **handoff mode**.
Work mode is dense and fast. Handoff mode strips to a single plain question, with the executive's workspace out of sight.

personas: Runs fifteen to twenty applications a day and owns the compliance on every one. Every extra tap costs them, and they need the handoff to be quick enough that it does not stall the conversation.
Same journey, no customer in the room
Drives the same flow over the phone, so the app and the call have to stay in step. Handoffs become links and OTPs rather than a passed device.
Owns the dealer portfolio, the team's pipeline and the escalations. They need status at a glance, not another data-entry screen.
deck.customerNote: The customer is not a user of this app. They are a participant in it, for the eight or so moments the law says only they can complete. Designing for them meant designing those moments, not a journey.
needs: **Fast for the person who lives in it.** Fifteen to twenty applications a day means every saved tap compounds.
**Instantly legible to someone who has never seen it.** The customer gets no training, no orientation and no second attempt.
**Safe to hand over.** The executive's phone holds other people's applications, and none of that can be visible when it changes hands.
firstRelease: **The eleven-step origination journey**, driven end to end by the executive.
**Handoff mode**: live photo, KYC and bureau consent, OTP, uploads, e-signature and home visit consent.
**Portfolio and dealer views** for store managers, built for reading rather than entry.
**A 100+ component library** the other five products build from.
themes: For the person who runs this all day, every tap is a cost. Work mode is dense on purpose.
At handoff a stranger has to understand what they are agreeing to with nobody explaining it.
The phone is not the customer's. Handoff shows them their step and nothing else.

dives.title: One screen, one job, because speed compounds.
bullets: Forty fields on a phone is a scroll nobody finishes twice, let alone twenty times a day.
So no screen asks for more than one category of information, and the executive never has to hunt for where they were.
This came out of testing, not theory. The first wireframes were scrollable and multi-action, and they lost everyone who tried them.
Dual progress, a percentage and a step count, so an executive interrupted mid-application knows exactly where to resume.

dives.title: The thirty seconds the customer is holding the phone.
bullets: At a handoff the screen changes character: one question, plain language, and what happens next stated before they act.
Live photo, KYC consent and the bureau check each say **why** the data is needed, not just that consent is required.
The key facts statement is signed by OTP, so the customer confirms with something only they have rather than a scrawl on a slip.
The executive's queue is hidden for the duration. Nobody hands a stranger a phone showing somebody else's loan.

dives.title: The one screen an executive shows rather than fills.
bullets: Amount, EMI, tenure and interest rate together, with the total cost stated rather than implied.
It is built to be read upside down across a desk, then turned around and read properly.
No fine print, no second screen, no charge that appears after the customer has committed.
This is what the whole journey is building toward, so it is the screen I spent longest on.

constraints: The phone is not the customer's

Handing over a device mid-application means handing over everything on it. Handoff mode hides the queue, locks navigation to the single step in front of the customer, and returns control to the executive when they are done.

KYC, bureau consent and the key facts statement are mandated and cannot be shortened. So I stopped fighting them and sequenced them instead: each lands at the moment it makes sense, never stacked into one wall at the end.
A flagship and an entry-level handset, same screens

The app had to hold up from a metro flagship to an entry-level Android on patchy rural coverage. That ruled out heavy imagery and animation, and it is why the interface leans on type, spacing and iconography that render at any size.

how.audit: I ran the paper process myself first, start to finish, as a fake customer in a real store, because reading a process document tells you nothing about what it feels like to sign six forms in front of someone who is waiting. Then a heuristic sweep of that plus five competitor apps, every issue rated 0 to 4 and tied to a specific role and task. The competitor teardown was task-matched rather than feature-matched: same job, five products, where does each one break.
how.personas: Built from shift observation, not interviews alone. I sat with executives through full days in three stores and counted: how many applications, how many interruptions, how often the phone changed hands. The store manager persona only emerged because the data showed they were reading far more than they were typing, which no one had said out loud in an interview.
how.wireframes: Grayscale, three options per hard screen, tested as printouts before anything was built. Executives ranked them against a timed task rather than saying which they liked. The scrolling multi-action layout won on preference and lost badly on time, which is the reason the whole product ended up as one screen per job.
how.validation: Two settings, deliberately. Figma prototypes with internal stakeholders and executives, which catches structure. Then I sat in an actual store and watched real customers take the phone at consent and signature steps, which catches everything the prototype cannot: that people sign without reading, that they hold the phone at an angle, that they hand it back too early. The second setting produced every change that mattered.

iterations: The first wireframes put several actions on one scrolling screen. Stakeholders and engineers both lost the thread. I pivoted the whole structure to one screen, one job, which became the rule the rest of the design hangs off.
Nobody could get back to a step they had finished

Six sales executives on the mid-fi prototype all hit the same wall: a completed step was a dead end. I added persistent edit affordances and a visible way back, so one wrong field no longer meant starting over.
Customers were signing things they had not read

Watching real handoffs was the uncomfortable part. People took the phone, saw a wall of compliance language, and tapped agree. Every handoff screen was rewritten to one plain question, the reason for it, and what happens next.
Handing the phone over exposed the queue
Testers could swipe out of the consent screen and into the executive's other applications. That is a privacy failure, not a UX nitpick. Handoff mode now locks to the single step until it is complete.

lessons.title: The handoff was the product. The rest was data entry.
bullets: **Design the seams, not just the screens.** The moments this app changes hands are the ones that carry legal weight, and they were the ones nobody had designed.
**Watch the room, not the prototype.** Sitting in a store and seeing a customer sign without reading told me more than any usability session.
**Consent is a design problem.** Legal decides what must be asked. How it is asked, and whether it is understood, is on me.
**Build the library first.** The component system is why five more products assembled in days. The screens were the visible part, not the valuable part.

v3.title: FinVista: Architecting an Assisted Lending Operating System at Scale

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Senior UX Lead (Product Architecture, Dual-Persona Workflows, Design System)

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: Rs 30,000+ Cr loan portfolio · 25M+ customer accounts · 500+ Indian cities

summary.h: Multi-day paper origination became an 11‑step operating system.
summary.p: FinVista transformed a multi-day paper origination process across India's largest NBFC network into an 11-step high-throughput native Android operating system. Ultimately, we reduced the loan processing turnaround time by 60 percent.

ps: Consumer lending apps optimise for single-user self-service. FinVista operates on a different paradigm: a single Android handset shared by a quota-driven field sales agent processing multiple applications simultaneously, and the actual borrower.
The borrower is a participant who takes over the device only for critical compliance moments: live photos, consents, OTPs and digital signatures.

context.h: Not quiet offices. Stockyards, dealer lots, budget phones.
context.p: Stepping into the UX Lead role, I quickly realised we were not designing for users in quiet office environments. The architecture was shaped by strict operational realities.

cards.d: Sales agents worked in outdoor vehicle stockyards and crowded dealership lots on company-issued budget phones with limited memory and inconsistent 4G.
A single loan application required agents to complete over 40 distinct data fields.
Two-Wheeler financing was the baseline, but the system had to scale across Consumer Durable, Personal, Used Car, Tractor and Three-Wheeler without engineering separate applications.

before.note: multi-day · consent re-captured · no offline state

after.note: 60% faster · local cache survives a dropped connection · one handset

innovation.p: The critical breakthrough came when I recognised we were designing for two entirely different personas sharing a single physical device. I engineered the application as an oscillating dual-state terminal governed by strict operational rules.

states.d: For sales agents processing 15 to 20 applications daily. Dense data entry, dedicated numeric keypads, maximum speed.

Regulation mandates the agent physically hand the device to the customer at multiple intervals. The moment they tap to hand over, the interface transforms: type scales to 18 point, internal dealership notes and risk scores are masked, and complexity gives way to plain language.
If the connection drops, local caching picks the application up exactly where it left off. No data loss during showroom walkarounds.

ps: To find the best way to input 40 data fields, we evaluated long scrolling forms and accordions. Both failed significantly on budget hardware: unpredictable viewport jumps and massive cognitive overload.

So I made the architectural decision to break the journey into an 11-step modular flow on a strict "one screen, one job" rule. It nominally increased the tap count and effectively reduced cognitive load to zero. Agents completed applications much faster because they always knew exactly what the screen in front of them wanted, whether scanning a PAN card or calculating an EMI.

journey.p: The eleven steps as the executive sees them, left to right. Two screens turn the phone around: the credit bureau consent and the key facts statement, where the borrower signs.

testing.h: Five rounds, 24 participants, tested on the real phones.
testing.p: To be sure the architecture would survive hostile field conditions, I ran five iterative rounds of moderated usability testing with high-fidelity Figma prototypes mirrored on budget Android devices. 24 participants: sales agents, store managers and actual borrowers.

metrics.l: Participants across agents, store managers and borrowers.
System Usability Scale, baseline to final round.

testing.frictionEye: Two friction points resolved before launch

friction.found: Agents struggled with continuous scrolling through 40 fields on one screen: visual fatigue, frequent input errors, viewport jumping on budget hardware.
friction.fixed: Replaced the long scroll with a progressive disclosure model. The 11-step flow presents one logical task at a time, which removed the scrolling friction and cut data entry errors.

friction.found: Once modular, agents lost their sense of where they were in the journey, and lengthy compliance checks bred anxiety without a sense of completion time.
friction.fixed: A dual progress indicator: a macro journey-level percentage combined with a micro step-level indicator. Transparent pacing kept users anchored.

scaling.h: The same 11 steps, reused across five more loan products.
ps: We were not just building a Two-Wheeler loan application. The architecture had to support Tractors, Used Cars and Consumer Durables.

I developed a design system of over 100 native Android components. With that unified architecture the exact 11-step logic was reused across five additional loan products. For Tractor loans we simply swapped urban salary inputs for land revenue records. That modularity saved engineering months of duplicated effort.

system.cap: Form controls: inputs, checkboxes, progress, toasts, file upload
Cards and sheets: lead cards, VAS cards, dialogs, bottom sheets

retro.p: Designing for shared devices in hostile environments yielded two critical technical learnings.

lessons.d: Subtle 1px light-grey dividers and low-contrast borders looked refined in design software and washed out completely under midday sun in outdoor stockyards. We overhauled the tokens for higher contrast ratios, bold borders and a 16sp minimum on all field inputs.

lessons.t: Designing for latency and button debouncing
lessons.d: Credit bureau and banking checks regularly hit 4 to 8 second latency spikes. Agents tapped submit repeatedly during freezes, firing duplicate verification calls. Deterministic optimistic loading skeletons and button debouncing eliminated the duplicates.

title: FinVista: Architecting an
Assisted Lending Operating System at Scale
v4.tags: Enterprise Fintech · Native Android · Assisted Lending · Design System · Field Operations
v4.deck: Loan applications used to take days and ran on paper. I rebuilt the whole thing as an eleven-step Android journey for one of India's largest NBFCs.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Senior UX Lead (Product Architecture, Dual-Persona Workflows, Design System)

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: Rs 30,000+ Cr loan portfolio · 25M+ customer accounts · 500+ Indian cities

ps: The same Android phone has to work for two different people. A field agent gets through fifteen to twenty applications a day on a cheap handset, usually standing in a stockyard on a 4G signal that keeps dropping. Then they hand that same phone to the borrower for the photo, the consents, the OTP and the signature. There are over forty fields to fill in for one application, and the whole thing had to work for six lending products without building six separate apps.

The app has two states and switches between them. When the agent is using it, it is dense and quick to fill in. When they hand the phone over, the type gets bigger, the language gets plainer, and the internal notes come off the screen. The journey is eleven steps with one job on each screen, and every field is saved to the phone as you go, so a dropped signal does not cost you anything. Underneath is a design system of over a hundred components that the other five loan products reused as it was.

lead.cap: The first two screens are what the agent sees. The third is what the borrower sees once the phone has been handed over.

sections.p: This was never going to be used in an office. The people using it are standing in vehicle stockyards and dealership lots, on company phones that cost about ten thousand rupees. Three things shaped the architecture:
cards: The phones were budget Android handsets with very little memory, and the 4G signal dropped constantly in outdoor stockyards and busy dealerships.
A single loan application needs more than forty separate pieces of information.
We built it for two-wheeler loans first, but consumer durables, personal loans, used cars, tractors and three-wheelers all had to run on the same system.

sections.p: These are the eleven steps in the order the agent works through them. On two of them the phone gets turned around: the credit bureau consent, and the key facts statement where the borrower signs.
sections.filmHint: Scroll sideways, and tap any screen to open it.

sections.h: The Core Innovation: Two Readers, One Screen
sections.p: The thing that unlocked it was realising two completely different people were sharing one device. The app switches between two states, and three rules govern how it behaves:
cards: The agent is doing fifteen to twenty of these a day, so this state is built for speed. The fields are packed in tight and the number pads are dedicated.
The agent taps to hand over and the screen changes. Type goes up to 18 point, the dealership notes and risk scores are hidden, the wording gets simpler, and there is one decision to make.
Every field is written to the phone as soon as it is filled in, so losing signal halfway round a showroom does not lose any of the work.

media.cap: On the left the agent is entering data. On the right the phone has been handed over for consent.

sections.h: Architecture: Why the 11‑Step Modular Stepper Won
sections.p: We tried long scrolling forms and we tried accordions, and both fell over on the cheap phones. The viewport jumped around unpredictably, and forty fields on one screen was more than anyone could hold in their head. So the journey became eleven separate steps with one job on each screen. It takes more taps that way, but nobody has to work out what to do next, and people finish faster.

items.alt: Layout exploration: long scroll, accordion, stepped wizard

media.cap: The layout options we tried: the long scroll, the accordion, and the stepped wizard that shipped.

sections.p: I ran five rounds of moderated testing before we committed to the architecture, using high-fidelity Figma prototypes mirrored onto the same budget Android phones people would be using.
sections.frictionTitle: Two friction points resolved before launch
friction: Scrolling through forty fields on one screen wore people out. They made more mistakes, and the viewport kept jumping on the cheaper phones.
We split it into the eleven-step flow, so there is one task on the screen at a time.
Once it was split into steps, agents lost track of where they were, and the longer compliance checks made people anxious.
We added two progress indicators side by side, one for how far through the whole journey you are and one for which step you are on.

items.alt: Progress exploration: top bar, vertical stepper, ring

media.cap: The progress options we looked at on the left. On the right, what shipped: the journey percentage and the step count together, on every screen.

sections.p: The architecture also had to handle tractors, used cars and consumer durables. A design system of more than a hundred native Android components carried the same eleven-step logic across five more loan products.
cards: Built on tokenised Material 3 foundations, covering colour, type, spacing, form controls, cards and sheets.
Tractor loans replaced the salary fields with land revenue records. The steps themselves stayed exactly the same.
Existing customers taking a durables or personal loan get a pre-approved journey, which brings the eleven steps down to four.

numbered: What looks good in Figma can be unreadable outdoors

The 1px light-grey dividers looked refined on my screen and disappeared completely under midday sun in a stockyard. I changed the tokens to higher contrast, heavier borders, and a 16sp minimum on every field.
Plan for the network being slow

Credit bureau and bank checks regularly took four to eight seconds. Agents assumed nothing had happened and tapped submit again, which fired duplicate calls. Loading skeletons and debounced buttons stopped that.
